paper: WiscKey: Separating Keys from Values in SSD-Conscious Storage
system_or_method: WiscKey: an LSM-tree-based persistent KV store (derived from LevelDB 1.18) that separates keys from values: keys + value addresses (<vLog-offset, value-size>) live in the LSM-tree; values are appended to a separate value log (vLog) as <key_size, value_size, key, value> tuples.
core_idea: Compaction in LSM-trees only needs to sort keys; values can be managed separately. WiscKey keeps only keys and 12-byte value locations in the LSM-tree and appends values to an unsorted vLog, cutting write amplification (from >12 to ~1 for >=1KB values) and shrinking the LSM-tree so it caches in RAM (100GB dataset -> ~2GB key tree, Sec 3.2). Unsorted values make range queries random-I/O-bound, which WiscKey mitigates with 32-thread parallel prefetch exploiting SSD internal parallelism; garbage in the vLog is reclaimed by an online GC that copies valid tail records to the head;
relation_to_vmemkv: Closest ancestor and the canonical key-value-separation paper. VMemKV's T1/T2 split is structurally WiscKey's LSM/vLog split with two substitutions: (a) the persistent key LSM-tree is replaced by a volatile RAM-resident sorted-array+append-region (T1), and (b) explicit read()/write()/fadvise I/O on the vLog is replaced by mmap with OS-delegated residency (T2). RocksDB BlobDB, VMemKV's planned baseline, is the productionized descendant of WiscKey.
same_as_vmemkv: (1) Metadata/value separation with a small index holding value offsets - T1 payload_bits(T2 offset) is exactly WiscKey's <vLog-offset, value-size> indirection (Sec 3.2, Fig 6). (2) The explicit argument that the key/metadata structure is small enough to be RAM-resident (100GB DB -> ~2GB key LSM "readily fits into main memory", Sec 3.2, p.5:10) - this is the core T1-in-RAM premise. (3) Value records stored with key + length header in the value file for GC validity checking (Fig 7: <key size, value size, key, value>) - matches VMemKV's T2 record header layout.
different_from_vmemkv: (1) WiscKey's key index is a persistent on-SSD LSM-tree with compaction, WAL-equivalent recovery, and snapshots; T1 is volatile RAM with binary-searched sorted region + append region and reorganization instead of compaction. (2) WiscKey does all value I/O with explicit syscalls (write buffering Sec 3.4.1, posix_fadvise Sec 3.5, 32-thread prefetch pool Sec 3.3.1/3.5) - it manages residency in user space via the page cache deliberately; VMemKV delegates T2 residency entirely to OS paging via mmap with no buffer pool. (3) WiscKey never updates values in place (pure append);
evaluated_workloads: db_bench microbenchmarks (Sec 4.2, key 16B, compression off): sequential load of 100GB across value sizes (Sec 4.2.1, Fig 9; LevelDB time breakdown Fig 10); random load (uniform) of 100GB across value sizes (Fig 11) with write amplification (Fig 12), 4KB random-write latency CDF (Fig 13), and per-level table-size breakdown (Fig 14); random lookup: 100K point lookups on the 100GB randomly loaded DB (Sec 4.2.2, Fig 15) with 4KB read-latency CDF (Fig 16); range query: 4GB scanned from a 100GB DB, both randomly loaded and sequentially loaded, across value sizes (Fig 17); garbage collection: random-load foreground while GC runs, free-space ratio 25-100%, 4KB KV pairs (Sec 4.2.3, Fig 18);
baselines: LevelDB (all microbenchmarks, Sec 4.2) and RocksDB with default configuration (YCSB only, Sec 4.3, Fig 21). Plus WiscKey's own worst-case variant with GC continuously running (Sec 4.3).
metrics: Throughput in MB/s (load, Figs 9, 11) and lookups/s / MB/s (Figs 15, 17) and K ops/s (YCSB, Fig 21); write amplification (Fig 4, Fig 12); read amplification (Fig 4, Sec 2.3); full latency CDFs for 4KB random writes (Fig 13) and 4KB random reads (Fig 16) - i.e., tail latency; LSM-tree size per level (Fig 14); throughput under background GC vs free-space ratio (Fig 18);
value_sizes: Key always 16B (Sec 4.2). Microbenchmark value-size sweep 64B to 256KB (Figs 9, 11, 12, 15, 17); 4KB fixed for latency CDFs (Figs 13, 16) and GC experiment (Sec 4.2.3); 1KB for amplification study (Sec 2.3, Fig 4), space amp (Fig 19), CPU (Fig 20), and recovery (Sec 4.2.4).
dataset_size_or_memory_ratio: 100GB database on a 64GB-RAM machine for all main experiments (Sec 4.1, 4.2, 4.3) - dataset ~1.6x DRAM, so the LevelDB/RocksDB block cache + page cache cannot hold everything, but WiscKey's ~2GB key LSM fully caches. Amplification motivation uses 1GB and 100GB DBs (Sec 2.3, Fig 4). No explicit memory-limit sweep (no 4x/8x dataset/memory ratios).
access_distribution: Microbenchmarks: uniform random (Sec 2.3 "keys randomly from a uniform distribution"; Sec 4.2.1 random load "uniformly distributed random order"). YCSB: Zipf for A, B, C, E, F; workload D uses a temporally weighted (latest) distribution (Fig 21 caption).
scan_or_range_support: Yes - Scan(start, end) in the API (Sec 3.1); implemented via iterator + 32-thread parallel vLog prefetch (Sec 3.3.1, 3.5). Evaluated in Fig 17 (4GB scanned from 100GB DB, random- and sequential-loaded, value-size sweep) and YCSB E (95% range queries of 1-100 pairs, Fig 21).
update_workload: YCSB A (50% updates on existing keys, Zipf), B (5% updates), F (50% read-modify-write) at 1KB and 16KB (Sec 4.3, Fig 21). GC experiment effectively an update/delete workload: load, delete 25-100% of pairs, random-load again under background GC (Sec 4.2.3, Fig 18).
larger_than_memory_setting: Partially: the 100GB dataset exceeds the 64GB DRAM (Sec 4.1), so values cannot all cache, and the paper's read-amplification analysis (Sec 2.3, Fig 4: read amp 8.2 -> 327 going from 1GB to 100GB because index/filter blocks stop caching) is exactly a larger-than-memory caching effect.
reason: Closest ancestor; fair re-implementation of 2016 LevelDB-based research code is impractical and RocksDB BlobDB is the runnable descendant. Its workload suite (value-size sweep, scan 3-state, GC-under-load, latency CDF, space amp) must be adopted; the system itself belongs in design comparison / responsibility table.
thesis_strengthening_points: (1) WiscKey empirically validates VMemKV's core premise: separating a small metadata plane from bulk values slashes write amplification (to ~1.14 predicted, ~1 measured for >=1KB values, Sec 3.2/Fig 12) and the metadata plane fits in RAM (Sec 3.2). (2) It legitimizes the T1-in-RAM design by showing the key structure for 100GB is ~2GB.
thesis_weakening_points: Be blunt: (1) NOVELTY RISK IS HIGH. 'RAM-resident index over a value file' is WiscKey's design with the LSM swapped for a sorted array; WiscKey already argued and exploited that the key structure caches entirely in RAM (Sec 3.2). The value-file record format (key+lengths header, Fig 7), offset-in-index indirection, and copy-live-records garbage reclamation are all in WiscKey. Even VMemKV's flagship differentiator - reorganizing the value log into key order - is explicitly proposed in WiscKey (p.5:20, and Introduction: 'can be improved by log reorganization'). VMemKV's defensible novelty narrows to: OS-delegated mmap residency (vs explicit I/O), in-place updates via alloc_len, and the RAM-native T1 structure;
reviewer_risk_if_omitted: Fatal if omitted or under-engaged: WiscKey is THE key-value separation paper and the direct ancestor of RocksDB BlobDB, VMemKV's chosen baseline. A reviewer will object that: (a) VMemKV's architecture is WiscKey with a volatile index and mmap, so the paper must cite it and articulate the delta explicitly; (b) T2 reorganization into key order was proposed in WiscKey (p.5:20) - failing to credit this reads as claiming WiscKey's future work as novel;
implementation_feasibility: Running WiscKey itself: low (unmaintained research code on LevelDB 1.18). Adopting its workloads: high once value-size knob and byte-scan API exist.
needs_verification: none for bibliography (TOS 13(1) 2017 printed in PDF)
notes: This is the TOS 2017 extended version (28 pages); it supersedes FAST'16 by adding latency CDFs (Figs 13, 16), the LSM-tree size breakdown (Fig 14), and expanded background - cite the TOS version if tail latency figures are referenced. Fig 20 is labeled a figure but is a CPU-usage table.

paper: RocksDB: Evolution of Development Priorities in a Key-value Store Serving Large-scale Applications
system_or_method: RocksDB (LSM-tree based embedded persistent key-value storage engine, SSD-optimized); the paper is an 8-year production retrospective on development priorities, not a new system.
category: LSM KVS experience/retrospective paper (production workload characterization, resource priorities, failure handling, configuration management, API lessons)
core_idea: An eight-year retrospective on RocksDB explaining how its optimization target evolved from write amplification to space amplification to CPU efficiency (Sec 3), driven by the observation that most production deployments are space-constrained rather than IOPS- or CPU-constrained (Fig 3). It distills operational lessons: per-host resource management across many co-located instances (Sec 4.1), configurable WAL treatment (Sec 4.3), backward/forward data-format compatibility (Sec 4.4), multi-layer checksumming because silent corruptions really occur (Sec 5), the burden of a huge tuning surface (Sec [...]
relation_to_vmemkv: Primary-baseline self-description and methodology source. VMemKV's planned evaluation uses RocksDB (and BlobDB, which this paper announces in Sec 3.5) as the main comparison system, so this paper defines what a fair, tuned RocksDB configuration looks like (compaction style, dynamic leveled compaction, bloom filters, block cache sizing, WAL modes, direct I/O, compression) and what production actually optimizes for (space, then CPU — not raw throughput).
same_as_vmemkv: (1) Key-value separation for large values: Sec 3.5 adds BlobDB, storing large objects separately to compact them less often — same motivation as VMemKV's T1/T2 split. (2) Recognition that block-table engines are inefficient for memory-resident data: Sec 8.1's mmap-able "plain tables" for Ramfs used byte addressing to avoid block lookups/copies, conceptually adjacent to VMemKV's mmap T2. (3) Both target variable-size values behind a compact index with bloom filters as an opt-in read optimization (Sec 2.2).
different_from_vmemkv: RocksDB implements its own buffer management (block cache + MemTables, managed via jemalloc, Sec 6.4) rather than delegating residency to the OS; it uses LSM compaction with multiple styles rather than whole-file reorganization; it provides WAL-based durability, multi-layer checksums (block, SSTable, handoff, planned per-KV, Fig 5, Sec 5.2-5.3), severity-classified error handling (Sec 5.4), backward/forward format compatibility (Sec 4.4), replication/backup support (Sec 4.2), transactions, merge operators and compaction filters (Sec 6.2), column families (Sec 2.2), and an enormous configuratio [...]
evaluated_workloads: This is an experience paper; measurements are micro-benchmarks plus production surveys, not a full benchmark suite: (1) random-write micro-benchmark comparing Leveled/Tiered/FIFO compaction, 500M keys, 16 B keys / 100 B values, populate then random overwrite at 2 MB/s ingestion, direct I/O, block cache = 10% of compacted DB size, RocksDB 5.9 (Table 3, Sec 2.2, p. 26:6); (2) space-efficiency micro-benchmark, pre-populated 200M-1B keys, random overwrites at constant 2 MB/s, default options, Dynamic Leveled vs LevelDB-style compaction (Table 4, Sec 3.2, p. 26:7); (3) production survey of write amplification vs write rate across 42 sampled ZippyDB/MyRocks applications (Fig 2, Sec 3.1);
baselines: Mostly self-comparison: Leveled vs Tiered vs FIFO compaction within RocksDB 5.9 (Table 3); Dynamic Leveled vs LevelDB-style compaction (Table 4); timestamp API vs application-encoded timestamps in keys (Table 6).
metrics: Write amplification, defined as total SSTable file writes vs MemTable bytes flushed, WAL excluded (Table 3 caption, Sec 2.2); average and max space overhead (Table 3); #I/O per Get() with and without bloom filter and #I/O per iterator seek (Table 3); steady-state DB size vs fully-compacted size and extra space overhead % (Table 4);
value_sizes: 100-byte values (about 50 bytes after compression) with 16-byte keys in the Table 3 micro-benchmark (Table 3 caption, p. 26:6). Value sizes not specified for Table 4 or Table 6 experiments. Production value-size distributions are not given here (delegated to Cao et al. FAST'20, ref [9]).
dataset_size_or_memory_ratio: Table 3: 500M keys, block cache sized to 10% of the fully compacted DB size, direct I/O (an effective 10:1 dataset:cache ratio, p. 26:6). Table 4: 200M-1B keys, compacted sizes 12.01-60.06 GB (p. 26:7). Production: >30 applications at Facebook storing "many hundreds of petabytes" (Sec 1). DRAM ratios never reported explicitly.
access_distribution: Uniform random for all micro-benchmarks: "random keys are overwritten" (Table 3 caption), "each write is to a key chosen randomly from the pre-populated key space" (Table 4 caption), DB_bench fill_seq/fill_random/read_random (Table 6). No Zipf/hotset distributions;
scan_or_range_support: Iterators/scans are a core API (Sec 2.2, Sec 7); scan cost is measured as #I/O per iterator seek in Table 3 (Leveled 1.84, Tiered 4.80, FIFO 967). Sec 6.3.1 documents the tombstone-scan pathology: production queries observed iterating over millions of tombstones to return a few KV pairs, with mitiga [...]
update_workload: Random overwrite of existing keys at a rate-limited 2 MB/s after full population (Tables 3 and 4); DB_bench read_while_writing (Table 6); merge operator described as the RMW mechanism, reducing write I/O but degrading reads since searches cannot stop at the first entry found (Sec 6.2.2).
larger_than_memory_setting: Not framed as an explicit larger-than-memory study, but Table 3 uses direct I/O with block cache capped at 10% of DB size, so reads are storage-bound (p. 26:6), and production datasets (hundreds of PB across fleets) trivially exceed DRAM.
reason: The expected primary production baseline. Current wrapper (default Options, Get-before-write, 8-byte value constraint, rocksdb_store.hpp:42-98) must be replaced by a fairness-configured wrapper (matched memory budget, stated WAL/compression/IO mode).
thesis_strengthening_points: (1) Sec 6.1/6.4 configuration and memory-management pain (Table 5: >25 configs across 39 deployments; block-cache-vs-MemTable sizing described as needing "significant experimentation"; jemalloc fragmentation 2-25%, Fig 6) is first-party evidence for VMemKV's core simplicity claim: OS-delegated residency removes exactly the knobs RocksDB users struggle with. (2) Sec 8.1's admission that block-based tables waste memory copies/lookups for memory-resident data, and that direct DRAM use is far more efficient, supports the RAM-resident T1 rationale.
thesis_weakening_points: (1) Wrong optimization target: the paper's central empirical claim is that production KV workloads are space-constrained (Sec 3.2, Fig 3), yet VMemKV's design worsens space amplification on two axes RocksDB spent years fixing — unreachable garbage accumulates in T2 until a whole-file reorganization, alloc_len padding adds internal fragmentation, and T2 is uncompressed while RocksDB compresses older levels (Sec 2.2; Table 3 shows 2x compression on 100 B values). If VMemKV cannot beat or match Dynamic Leveled's ~13% steady-state overhead (Table 4), the design loses on the metric that matters most in production.
reviewer_risk_if_omitted: A reviewer who knows this paper will attack on five fronts if it is ignored. (1) "You measured throughput/latency but the RocksDB team's own retrospective shows production is space-constrained (Fig 3) — where is your space amplification result, and how does uncompressed T2 with reorganization-deferred garbage compare to Dynamic Leveled's 13% (Table 4)?" (2) "Your simplicity/responsibility table is unfair: Sec 1 and Sec 5 show RocksDB's complexity buys checksums, crash consistency, compatibility, and error handling that your MAP_PRIVATE, fsync-free implementation simply lacks — compare against [...]
implementation_feasibility: High (librocksdb packaged; wrapper exists and needs option surface + BlobDB).
notes: This is the ACM TOS journal extension of the FAST'21 paper "Evolution of Development Priorities in Key-value Stores Serving Large-scale Applications: The RocksDB Experience" (Sec 9 lists the added material: column families, callbacks, deletion optimization, memory management, column support, failed initiatives).

paper: Are You Sure You Want to Use MMAP in Your Database Management System?
system_or_method: Position/analysis paper (no new system): experimental analysis of mmap-based file I/O vs. traditional buffer-pool-style direct I/O (fio O_DIRECT), plus a catalog of correctness and performance failure modes of mmap in DBMSs.
category: mmap criticism / anti-mmap position paper with microbenchmark evaluation
core_idea: mmap is not a suitable replacement for a DBMS buffer pool. It has four problem classes (Sec 3): (1) transactional safety — the OS can flush dirty pages at any time, forcing complicated OS-CoW / user-space-CoW / shadow-paging protocols; (2) I/O stalls — no async reads, any access can block on a page fault, and mlock/madvise workarounds are limited; (3) error handling — checksum validation on every access, silent persistence of corrupted pages, SIGBUS signal handling;
relation_to_vmemkv: The central criticism source. VMemKV's T2 design (OS-delegated page residency of an mmap-backed value file, no user-space buffer pool) is exactly the pattern this paper argues against. It is simultaneously VMemKV's most important methodology source: the fio O_DIRECT baseline, the TLB-shootdown measurement via /proc/interrupt, the time-series eviction-onset plots, and the madvise-mode ablation define the experiments a reviewer will expect VMemKV to run.
same_as_vmemkv: (a) Both concern larger-than-memory data via mmap with OS-managed residency (Sec 1, Sec 2.1). (b) Both use madvise hints: VMemKV's MemoryHints issues MADV_SEQUENTIAL before scans; the paper analyzes MADV_NORMAL/RANDOM/SEQUENTIAL (Sec 2.2, Sec 4). (c) VMemKV currently uses MAP_PRIVATE on T2; the paper explicitly describes MAP_PRIVATE semantics (changes not persisted to the backing file, Sec 2.2) and its use in MongoDB MMAPv1's OS copy-on-write update protocol (Sec 3.1).
different_from_vmemkv: (a) The paper attacks mmap as a full buffer-pool replacement for page-oriented DBMSs; VMemKV mmaps only the T2 value log while keeping the entire control plane (T1 index, hashes, offsets, bloom filter) RAM-resident, so index traversal never page-faults and at most one T2 access per Get touches faultable memory. (b) The paper is a pure measurement/position paper with fio microbenchmarks — no KV API, no YCSB, no system built. (c) The paper's experiments are exclusively read-only ("the best-case scenario for mmap", Sec 4); VMemKV evaluates updates, reorganization, and garbage reclamation.
evaluated_workloads: Only two read-only microbenchmark access patterns, both over a 2 TB raw SSD range: (1) Random reads, 100 threads, simulating a larger-than-memory OLTP workload (Sec 4.1, Fig 2a bandwidth in reads/s, Fig 2b TLB shootdowns/s), comparing fio O_DIRECT pread vs mmap with MADV_NORMAL / MADV_RANDOM (MADV_RND) / MADV_SEQUENTIAL (MADV_SEQ). (2) Sequential scan: 1 SSD (Sec 4.2, Fig 3; mmap 20 threads, fio libaio 1 thread iodepth 256) and 10 SSDs in software RAID 0 via md (Sec 4.2, Fig 4; mmap 20 threads, fio libaio 4 threads iodepth 256). All runs are ~60-second time series.
baselines: fio v3.25 [ref 2] with direct I/O (O_DIRECT) bypassing the OS page cache: O_DIRECT pread for random reads (Fig 2), O_DIRECT libaio with iodepth 256 for sequential scans (Figs 3-4). Compared against mmap under three madvise modes (MADV_NORMAL, MADV_RANDOM, MADV_SEQUENTIAL).
metrics: (1) Random reads per second over time (Fig 2a). (2) TLB shootdowns per second over time, measured via /proc/interrupt (Fig 2b; peaks around 1.5-2.0M/s on the axis). (3) Sequential-scan bandwidth in GB/s over time (Fig 3: 0-6 GB/s axis for 1 SSD; Fig 4: 0-60 GB/s axis for 10 SSDs). Qualitative observations: kswapd single process CPU-bound during eviction;
value_sizes: not specified — the benchmark reads raw pages, not KV records. 4 KB OS pages are the implied granularity (Sec 2.2 notes MADV_NORMAL reads 128 KB = accessed page + next 16 + previous 15 pages at 4 KB pages).
dataset_size_or_memory_ratio: 2 TB SSD range vs 100 GB available Linux page cache = 20x dataset/memory ratio; "95% of all accesses resulted in page faults (i.e., the workload was I/O-bound)" (Sec 4.1). Machine: single-socket AMD EPYC 7713 (64 cores / 128 HW threads), 512 GB RAM of which 100 GB was available to Linux v5.11 for its page cache;
access_distribution: Uniform random over the 2 TB range for the random-read experiment (Sec 4.1; no skew/Zipf used) and pure sequential for the scan experiments (Sec 4.2). No hot-set, Zipfian, or latest distributions evaluated.
scan_or_range_support: Sequential scan is one of the two evaluated patterns (Sec 4.2, Figs 3-4): fio libaio sustains full device bandwidth on 1 SSD; mmap matches fio for ~17 s until the page cache fills, then collapses;
update_workload: Not evaluated. Explicitly read-only "best-case scenario for mmap" because writes would require the complex update protections of Sec 3.1 that "incur substantial additional overhead [30]" (Sec 4).
larger_than_memory_setting: Yes — the core setting. 2 TB working range over 100 GB page cache (20x), so eviction is continuous after warm-up (Sec 4.1). Key behavior: eviction onset is a phase change — mmap MADV_RANDOM matched fio for the first ~27 s (cache filling), dropped to nearly zero for ~5 s, then recovered to ~half of fio's throughput (Sec 4.1, Fig 2a);
reason: Not a system to race but the criticism VMemKV must answer with its own measurements: fio O_DIRECT device-bound line, 60s+ eviction-onset time series, TLB shootdown series, madvise ablation. Methodology source of the highest priority.
thesis_strengthening_points: (1) The paper concedes a legitimate mmap regime: "your working set (or the entire database) fits in memory and the workload is read-only" (Sec 6) — VMemKV can claim it widens this regime by keeping all metadata in RAM (T1) so only value bytes are faultable, and Inline64/BloomFilter/AppendMap avoid touching T2 at all for small values and negative lookups; a full mmap-buffer-pool DBMS faults on index pages too, which is precisely what the paper measured.
thesis_weakening_points: Adversarial reading: (1) The paper's verdict is categorical — for larger-than-memory workloads with updates and durability needs, "Otherwise, never" (Sec 6). VMemKV's planned headline setting (4x/8x larger-than-memory, YCSB A/F with updates) checks every "do not use mmap" box: transactionally safe updates (bullet 1), no blocking on slow I/O (bullet 2), error handling (bullet 3), high throughput on fast storage (bullet 4). (2) Even in mmap's best case (read-only, correct hint), throughput fell to ~50% of direct I/O after eviction onset with a near-zero 5-second trough (Fig 2a) — if VMemKV loses to RocksDB/BlobDB by ~2x at 4x-8x memory ratios on reads, the thesis's "practical performance" claim collapses to "practical only below memory capacity", which is the paper's position restated.
reviewer_risk_if_omitted: Maximal — this is the paper every systems reviewer will cite in the first paragraph of a review of an mmap-based KV store. If VMemKV does not (a) cite it, (b) reproduce or confront the eviction-onset cliff and TLB shootdown storm on its own hardware, (c) include a direct-I/O (fio O_DIRECT) bound, and (d) answer the transactional-safety argument (dirty-page writeback vs WAL ordering; MAP_PRIVATE non-persistence; mlock impotence), the paper reads as unaware of a famous, directly on-point negative result and will be rejected on that basis alone.
implementation_feasibility: High for adopting methodology (fio + /proc/interrupts + time series); TLB attribution unreliable inside VMs - prefer bare metal.
notes: Short 6-page CIDR paper; pdftotext -layout output was clean and complete, including all figures' captions and both reference columns. Figure numbers verified: Fig 1 (mmap access walkthrough), Table 1 (mmap-based DBMSs and years), Fig 2a/2b (random reads, 1 SSD, 100 threads), Fig 3 (scan, 1 SSD), Fig 4 (scan, 10 SSDs).

system_or_method: vmcache (user-space buffer manager using anonymous mmap + explicit pread/pwrite + MADV_DONTNEED for DBMS-controlled eviction, 64-bit page-state array with optimistic/shared/exclusive locking, clock replacement, variable page sizes) plus exmap (Linux kernel module for batched, TLB-shootdown-free, loc [...]
category: Buffer manager / DBMS-OS co-design (virtual-memory-based page cache with DBMS-retained eviction control; explicit anti-mmap position)
core_idea: Use hardware virtual memory (page table + TLB) as the PID-to-pointer translation mechanism of a buffer pool, but WITHOUT file-backed mmap: the DBMS maps an anonymous region the size of storage, explicitly preads pages into it on a miss, and explicitly evicts with MADV_DONTNEED, so the DBMS keeps full control over faulting, eviction, and write-back (Sec 3).
relation_to_vmemkv: Direct intellectual opponent and the single most dangerous related-work item. vmcache takes exactly the opposite trade-off to VMemKV's T2: it argues (Sec 1, Sec 2, Table 1) that OS-delegated residency (file-backed mmap) is fundamentally flawed — loss of eviction control breaks ARIES-style WAL, no async I/O, unpredictable stalls, and Linux VM is too slow for NVMe — and builds a design where the DBMS keeps control while still using virtual memory for translation.
same_as_vmemkv: Both use virtual memory / mmap-family primitives so that cache hits are plain TLB-translated memory accesses with no user-space buffer-pool hash table on the hit path (vmcache Sec 3; VMemKV T2). Both argue simplicity of implementation as a selling point (vmcache Table 1 "implem. easy"; abstract "easy to implement"). Both use madvise-family hints as a control channel to the kernel (vmcache: MADV_DONTNEED for eviction; VMemKV: MADV_SEQUENTIAL/MADV_HUGEPAGE as opt-in hints).
different_from_vmemkv: (1) Control: vmcache's whole point is that the DBMS retains page-fault and eviction control (anonymous mapping + explicit pread + MADV_DONTNEED); VMemKV delegates T2 residency entirely to the OS via file-backed mmap — the design vmcache Sec 2 explicitly rejects. (2) Granularity/object model: vmcache caches fixed 4 KB (or multiple-of-4 KB) pages under a B+tree; VMemKV stores variable-size value records in a log-like value file with a separate sorted/append T1 index. (3) Kernel involvement: full vmcache performance requires the exmap kernel module; VMemKV is pure user space by design.
evaluated_workloads: 1) In-memory scalability, 1-128 threads: random point lookups (100 M entries ≈ 20 GB, 8-byte uniform keys, 120-byte values) and TPC-C (200 warehouses ≈ 40 GB), 128 GB pool (Sec 5.1-5.2, Fig 6). 2) Out-of-memory over time: random lookups (5 B entries ≈ 1 TB) and TPC-C (5000 warehouses ≈ 1 TB) against a 128 GB pool at 128 threads, throughput and read/write GB/s vs fio-measured I/O bound over 200 s (Sec 5.3, Fig 7). 3) Page-access microbenchmark: random 4 KB page reads in 32 KB and 128 GB arrays, incrementally adding 1 TB VM range, page-state access, version check, vs open-addressing hash table (Sec 5.4, Table 2).
baselines: LeanStore (pointer swizzling, 8 page-provider threads), WiredTiger 3.2.1 (pointer swizzling, 32 KB leaf pages), LMDB 0.9.24 (file-backed mmap, out-of-place writes, single writer) — all as standalone C++-linked storage engines with WAL disabled and lowest isolation (Sec 5.1).
metrics: Transactions/s and lookups/s vs thread count (Fig 6); throughput over time and read/write/total I/O GB/s vs fio-measured I/O bound (Fig 7); instructions, cache misses, and access latency ns per page access (Table 2); alloc+free operations/s (Figs 3, 8, 10 left); reads/s from null_blk (Fig 10 right); read throughput GiB/s and threads-to-saturation (Fig 9);
value_sizes: 120-byte values with 8-byte keys for the key/value random-lookup workload (Sec 5.1); TPC-C tuple sizes (standard, not itemized). No large-value (KiB-scale) experiments.
dataset_size_or_memory_ratio: In-memory: 20 GB (lookup) and 40 GB (TPC-C) vs 128 GB pool (Fig 6). Out-of-memory: ≈1 TB datasets (5 B entries; 5000 warehouses) vs 128 GB pool ⇒ ≈8x data/memory, described as "larger than the buffer pool by one order of magnitude" (Sec 5.3, Fig 7).
access_distribution: Uniformly-distributed 8-byte keys, random point lookups (Sec 5.1); TPC-C's standard access pattern ("complex access patterns and write-heavy", Sec 5.1). No Zipf/hot-set experiments.
scan_or_range_support: Supported in principle (B+tree engine; Table 1 argues page-table translation supports next-pointers in B+tree leaves that swizzling struggles with) but no scan/range workload is evaluated.
update_workload: TPC-C is the write-heavy workload (Sec 5.1; Figs 6, 7). Dirty pages are written back in batches of up to 64 pages via libaio during eviction (Sec 3.4, Sec 5.1). No dedicated update/RMW/blind-write microbenchmark; no YCSB A/F equivalents.
larger_than_memory_setting: Yes, central: Sec 5.3 / Fig 7 runs ≈1 TB datasets against a 128 GB buffer pool (≈8x) at 128 threads, plotting throughput over 200 s from load to steady state plus read/write I/O GB/s against an fio-measured I/O bound.
reason: Buffer manager, not a standalone KVS; VMemKV claims no performance win over DBMS-controlled designs. Adopt its methodology: fio-bound I/O plots (Fig 7), kernel flame graph (Fig 4), Table-2-style hit-path ablation, DRAM overhead accounting (Sec 3.6). Compare responsibilities (no eviction decisions, no frame table), not throughput.
thesis_strengthening_points: 1) Table 2 (Sec 5.4) empirically validates VMemKV's core premise: TLB-translated access to a huge mapped region costs almost nothing extra in-memory (<8% over raw DRAM read; +7% TLB pressure going from 128 GB to a 1 TB VM range), and hash-table translation (what a user-space buffer pool over T2 would need) is ~40% slower per access — so delegating hit-path translation to hardware/OS is defensible. 2) vmcache needs a custom kernel module (exmap) to fully exploit one fast SSD;
thesis_weakening_points: This paper is a direct, published, SIGMOD-level argument that VMemKV's central design decision (OS-delegated T2 residency) is wrong for exactly VMemKV's target regime. Specifics: (1) Table 1 and Sec 2 classify OS-controlled mmap caching as slow out-of-memory and state that lack of eviction control 'is a fundamental problem' that 'prevents the implementation of ARIES-style transactions' — VMemKV's paper-design durability (WAL before update over a MAP_SHARED mmap T2) has precisely the broken write-ordering vmcache describes: the kernel may write back a dirty T2 page before the WAL record is durable, and no stock interface prevents it.
reviewer_risk_if_omitted: Very high — this is arguably the paper VMemKV cannot omit. It is by Leis et al. (also authors of the Crotty mmap-criticism paper VMemKV must confront), published at SIGMOD 2023, and it (a) enumerates the four canonical failures of OS-delegated mmap caching, (b) empirically shows the Linux VM subsystem saturating at 1.5 M page ops/s with 79% TLB-shootdown CPU time, (c) shows the mmap-based LMDB losing across the board, and (d) demonstrates that DBMS-controlled, VM-assisted caching is simultaneously fast, scalable, AND easy to implement — undercutting VMemKV's simplicity differentiator.

paper: LeanStore: A High-Performance Storage Engine for NVMe SSDs
system_or_method: LeanStore: an embeddable OLTP storage engine for NVMe SSDs and multi-core CPUs. Components: buffer management via pointer swizzling, transitioning to vmcache (virtual-memory-assisted buffer management with DBMS-controlled eviction via mmap(MAP_ANONYMOUS)+pread+madvise(MADV_DONTNEED));
category: Buffer manager / SSD-optimized transactional storage engine (explicit pro-buffer-manager, anti-OS-paging position paper with architecture overview)
core_idea: Neither in-memory systems nor traditional disk-based systems can exploit modern NVMe SSDs; a storage engine can rival in-memory performance without keeping all data in RAM by combining in-memory optimizations (optimistic synchronization, cache efficiency) with disk-based techniques (B-trees, paged storage, physiological logging, fuzzy checkpoints). The buffer manager indirection can be made near-zero-overhead — first via pointer swizzling, now via vmcache, which uses the CPU's virtual-memory hardware for page translation while keeping eviction and replacement under DBMS control.
relation_to_vmemkv: Primary adversarial position paper and the strongest intellectual competitor camp. LeanStore/vmcache occupies the exact opposite design point on VMemKV's central axis: it explicitly rejects OS-controlled page residency (file-backed mmap) and argues the DBMS must control eviction, while VMemKV's T2 delegates residency to the OS. It is also: (a) a methodology source (Fig 4 instruction-per-transaction component breakdown, following Harizopoulos et al.);
same_as_vmemkv: Same goal: near-in-memory performance on larger-than-memory data without keeping everything in RAM (Sec 2, p.4537). Same simplicity ideology: paper closes with Wirth's "plea for lean software" and reports repeated rewrites for radical simplification (Sec 3, p.4543); it also values "fewer configuration parameters" (Sec 1, p.4537). Same API scope: embeddable library with insert, update, delete, point lookup, range scan; keys/payloads are opaque byte arrays (Sec 2, p.4537).
different_from_vmemkv: 1) Residency control: vmcache deliberately does NOT use file-backed mmap because "the operating system (OS) controls paging and eviction, causing major semantical and performance issues" (Sec 2.1, p.4538, endorsing Crotty et al. [14]); the DBMS explicitly evicts via madvise(MADV_DONTNEED) and reads via pread. VMemKV's T2 is exactly the rejected design. 2) LeanStore is transactional (MVCC/snapshot isolation, OSIC commit, Sec 2.6) with fully implemented durability: decentralized GSN logging, continuous fuzzy checkpoints, parallel bounded recovery (Sec 2.7);
evaluated_workloads: This overview paper contains exactly one experiment: TPC-C Neworder transaction, run in-memory with 1 thread, measuring x86 machine instructions per transaction with a component breakdown (logging, locking, latching, buffer manager, B-tree inefficiency, useful work), following the Harizopoulos et al. "OLTP Through the Looking Glass" methodology of removing components one at a time (Sec 3 "OLTP Through The Looking Glass Revisited", Fig 4, p.4543). Figures 1 and 3 are hardware trend data (DRAM/SSD/disk prices; x86 core counts), not workloads.
baselines: Shore (traditional disk-based storage engine) in Fig 4 (Sec 3, p.4543). PostgreSQL is cited as "completely CPU-bound on out-of-memory OLTP workloads" on NVMe but via reference [23], not measured here (Sec 1, p.4536). No other baselines evaluated in this paper.
metrics: x86 machine instruction count per TPC-C Neworder transaction, decomposed by component (Fig 4, p.4543). Qualitative/cited-only metrics: CPU cycles per page-value computation (~100 cycles, Sec 2.2, p.4539), CPU-cycle budget per I/O (15,000 cycles, Sec 2.3, p.4539), IOPS capability of PCIe 5.0 SSDs (~3M random 4KB reads, Sec 2.3, p.4539).
value_sizes: not specified (TPC-C schema implied for Fig 4; no explicit value sizes anywhere in the paper).
dataset_size_or_memory_ratio: not specified; the only experiment (Fig 4) is explicitly in-memory. Out-of-memory performance is claimed only via citation [24] (Sec 3, p.4543: "capable of achieving similar performance in out-of-memory workloads [24]").
access_distribution: not specified beyond TPC-C's inherent distribution; skewed workloads discussed qualitatively for page replacement (Sec 2.2, p.4538: ARC/LRU-k "result in better hit rates for skewed, real-world workloads") but not evaluated in this paper.
scan_or_range_support: Range scan is part of the API (Sec 2, p.4537: "insert, update, delete, point lookup, range scan") and B-trees provide ordered access; scans are NOT evaluated in this paper.
update_workload: TPC-C Neworder (Fig 4) contains inserts/updates as part of the transaction mix; no dedicated update/RMW/blind-write microbenchmark in this paper. Write handling is treated architecturally: WATT tracks writes separately (8 read + 4 write timestamps per page) because flash writes are slower than reads [...]
larger_than_memory_setting: Not evaluated in this paper (Fig 4 is in-memory, single-thread). Larger-than-memory capability is the system's core claim but supported only by citations: PostgreSQL CPU-bound out-of-memory [23] (Sec 1, p.4536); "similar performance in out-of-memory workloads [24]" (Sec 3, p.4543);
reason: TPC-C transactional storage engine; out of KVS scope. Must be cited because it answers the "buffer managers are heavy" motivation (Fig 4) - VMemKV may not use buffer-pool cost as motivation, only responsibility count.
thesis_strengthening_points: 1) LeanStore concedes the cost of DBMS-controlled residency: it had to rewrite the entire I/O path, disable the OS page cache and filesystem, adopt SPDK, and "re-implement many of the I/O and scheduling responsibilities operating systems are supposed to handle" (Sec 2.3, p.4539) — this is exactly the implementation-responsibility burden VMemKV's thesis says can be delegated; VMemKV's comparison table can cite this sentence directly. 2) The paper's own simplicity ideology (Wirth quote, repeated rewrites for simplification, Sec 3, p.4543;
thesis_weakening_points: This paper is close to a point-by-point refutation of VMemKV's premise, from the group that has published most on this exact question. (1) It explicitly rejects OS-controlled eviction: file-backed mmap "caus[es] major semantical and performance issues for database systems [14]" (Sec 2.1, p.4538) — the "semantical" issues (no write control, no durability ordering) are visible in VMemKV's current code (MAP_PRIVATE, no msync), so VMemKV currently instantiates the criticized design including its known failure mode. (2) VMemKV's motivating claim that buffer managers are complex/expensive is answered head-on: Fig 4 (p.4543) shows buffer-manager overhead engineered to a small slice, useful work dominant, and 10x higher in-memory performance than Shore;
reviewer_risk_if_omitted: Very high — this is the paper (with its companions vmcache [43], Haas&Leis [24], and Crotty et al. [14]) that any storage-engine reviewer will use to frame VMemKV. If omitted: (a) the motivation section will be called stale, since 'buffer manager overhead' was answered by Fig 4 and by the explicit claim that every modern DBMS needs a buffer manager (Sec 2.1);

paper: Faster: A Concurrent Key-Value Store with In-Place Updates
system_or_method: FASTER: a concurrent latch-free hash index (fully RAM-resident, 8-byte entries, keys NOT stored in index) paired with HybridLog, a record log spanning memory and SSD divided into a mutable in-place-update region (in-memory tail), a read-only region (in-memory, RCU-on-update), and a stable region (on [...]
category: Hybrid-log KVS (hash-index + log spanning memory/storage, in-place updates, point operations only)
core_idea: Log-structured (read-copy-update) designs limit throughput for update-intensive workloads, so FASTER combines a cache-optimized latch-free hash index with HybridLog: the in-memory tail of the log is a mutable region where hot records are updated in-place, while colder records transition through a read-only region (second-chance cache) to disk via RCU. This shapes memory contents like a second-chance FIFO cache without any per-record/per-page statistics, and the system explicitly manages its own bounded circular buffer (no OS delegation, no traditional buffer pool with page latching).
relation_to_vmemkv: Direct competitor/ancestor in the "RAM-resident index + larger-than-memory record store with in-place updates" design space, and the strongest counter-argument to OS-delegated residency: FASTER deliberately manages memory in user space (epoch-protected circular buffer, explicit head/read-only/tail offsets, async I/O) rather than delegating to the OS, and shows this yields 100M+ ops/sec.
same_as_vmemkv: (1) Fully RAM-resident compact index/control plane separated from record storage: FASTER keeps keys out of the index precisely to "retain it entirely in memory" (Sec 2.1), analogous to VMemKV's T1. (2) In-place update when possible, out-of-place append when not: FASTER updates in-place in the mutable region and appends (RCU) otherwise (Sec 6.1, Table 1/2); VMemKV updates in-place when new_value_len <= alloc_len, else appends to T2.
different_from_vmemkv: (1) Memory management ownership: FASTER explicitly manages residency in user space via a bounded in-memory circular buffer with head/read-only/tail offsets, epoch-triggered async flush and eviction (Sec 5.1-5.2, 6.1); VMemKV delegates T2 residency entirely to the OS via mmap. FASTER never blocks a thread on a fault — misses become async I/O requests with pending-operation continuations (Sec 5.3, Appendix G); VMemKV threads block synchronously on major page faults. (2) No ordered structure at all: hash-only, no range scans (Sec 1.1 dismisses them;
evaluated_workloads: All from extended YCSB-A, 250M distinct 8-byte keys (Sec 7.1): (1) Single-thread YCSB-A variants 0:100 RMW, 0:100 blind-write, 50:50, 100:0 read-only, 8-byte payloads, uniform and Zipf (Sec 7.2.1, Fig 8a/8b). (2) Same variants on all 56 threads (Sec 7.2.2, Fig 8c/8d). (3) Thread-scalability 1-56 threads, Zipf: 100% RMW 8-byte payloads (Fig 9a) and 0:100 blind update 100-byte payloads (Fig 9b) (Sec 7.2.3). (4) Redis microbenchmark: redis-benchmark, 8-byte values, 20M get/set, pipeline 1-200 (Sec 7.2.4). (5) Larger-than-memory: 27GB dataset, 100-byte payloads, 14 threads, 50:50 Zipf and 0:100 blind update vs memory budget (Sec 7.3, Fig 10);
baselines: Masstree (pure in-memory range index) and Intel TBB concurrent hash map (pure in-memory hash) for in-memory workloads; RocksDB (WAL and checksums disabled, direct I/O, RocksDB-Wiki-recommended params, 10-min runs) for larger-than-memory; Redis evaluated separately via redis-benchmark (Sec 7.1, 7.2.4).
metrics: Throughput in M ops/sec (Figs 8-11); scalability vs #threads (Fig 9, 11, 13); throughput vs memory budget (Fig 10); log growth rate MB/sec (Fig 12a); percentage of fuzzy (pending) operations (Figs 12b, 13); cache miss ratio in simulation (Figs 14-16); sequential log write bandwidth GB/sec (Sec 7.3 text). NO latency metrics at all (no average, no p99), no page-fault/TLB/CPU counters.
value_sizes: 8 bytes and 100 bytes only (Sec 7.1). 8-byte keys. Larger-than-memory experiments use 100-byte payloads (Sec 7.3). No KiB-scale values anywhere.
dataset_size_or_memory_ratio: In-memory experiments: 250M keys x 8B or 100B values, fitting in 256GB RAM (Sec 7.1, 7.2). Larger-than-memory: 27GB core dataset, memory budget swept along x-axis of Fig 10 (0-45GB range shown), with 2GB of the budget reserved for the hash index sized at #keys/8 buckets (Sec 7.3) — i.e., ratios from well above 1x dataset/memory down to fully in-mem [...]
access_distribution: Uniform; Zipfian theta = 0.99 (Sec 7.1); custom "hot set" distribution modeling drift — a shifting hot set of 1/5 of keys accessed with 90% probability, cold set with 10% (Sec 7.1, Sec 7.5, Fig 16 — used in the caching simulation).
scan_or_range_support: Not supported and not evaluated. FASTER is a point-operations store; Sec 1.1 explicitly argues range queries are infrequent for target apps and "can be served with simple workarounds such as indexing histograms of key ranges." Runtime interface has only Read/Upsert/RMW/Delete (Sec 2.2, Appendix E).
update_workload: Central to the paper. Blind updates (upserts) and read-modify-writes are first-class: YCSB-A variants 0:100 blind-write, 50:50, and 100% RMW (increment-by-input modeling per-key running sum) (Sec 7.1, Fig 8, Fig 9); larger-than-memory 50:50 and 0:100 blind update (Sec 7.3, Fig 10);
larger_than_memory_setting: Yes: Sec 7.3, Fig 10. 27GB dataset, 100-byte payloads, 14 threads on one socket, memory budget varied (2GB reserved for hash index). 50:50 Zipf: FASTER "slows down with limited memory because of increased random reads from SSD, but quickly reaches in-memory performance levels once the entire dataset fits in memory," with an acknowledged "steep perf [...]
reason: Point-ops-only store (no scans) so not a natural primary rival, but open-source C++ and the title owner of larger-than-memory in-place updates. Adopt: memory-budget sweep (Fig 10), R:U ratio variants, hot-set drift, in-place-vs-append ablation (Fig 11). Do NOT differentiate on in-place update; differentiate on file-backed OS residency.
thesis_strengthening_points: (1) No range scans: FASTER explicitly dismisses range queries (Sec 1.1) and its interface has no scan (Sec 2.2, Appendix E) — VMemKV's sorted T1 region + ordered Scan (and YCSB-E) occupies a gap FASTER cannot serve; this is VMemKV's cleanest differentiation. (2) Small values only: 8B/100B payloads throughout (Sec 7.1); FASTER's unified log copies the whole record on every RCU, which would be punishing at 16 KiB values — supports VMemKV's key-value separation with OS-cached large values as a distinct design point.
thesis_weakening_points: (1) FASTER is a direct existence proof that the alternative to OS delegation — explicit user-space residency management with async I/O — achieves up to 160M ops/sec and 'exceeds pure in-memory data structures' (Abstract, Sec 7.2). VMemKV's central claim that delegating residency to the OS is a good trade must survive the question: FASTER already showed user-space management wins on performance, so VMemKV's only remaining currency is simplicity + scans, and it must quantify what OS delegation costs. (2) Synchronous blocking: FASTER converts every storage miss into async I/O and keeps threads busy (Sec 5.3, Algs 2-4); VMemKV threads block in the kernel on every major fault.
reviewer_risk_if_omitted: Very high. FASTER is the canonical citation for (a) larger-than-memory point-operation KVS with a fully RAM-resident hash index, (b) in-place updates as the key to update-intensive performance, and (c) statistics-free memory shaping. If VMemKV omits it, reviewers will conclude the authors don't know the closest prior work: the novelty claims around 'RAM-resident control plane + larger-than-memory values + in-place updates' read as FASTER-with-mmap.
implementation_feasibility: Adopting workloads: high. Running FASTER C++: medium (open source; Windows-first heritage, Linux build exists).
notes: Full 16-page PDF (main body Secs 1-9 plus Appendices A-G) extracted cleanly with pdftotext -layout. Caveats worth carrying into the related-work text: (1) the headline 160M number is the Zipf all-threads figure rounded (Sec 7.2.2 text says 165M for Zipf, abstract says 'up to 160M');

paper: From FASTER to F2: Evolving Concurrent Key-Value Store Designs for Large Skewed Workloads
system_or_method: F2 (FASTER v2): a concurrent, latch-free, hash-indexed two-tier log KV store (hot log + cold log + read-cache), C++, ~11k SLOC, open-source in the FASTER repo.
category: Hybrid-log hash-based KVS for larger-than-memory skewed workloads (evolution of FASTER; explicit user-space memory/I-O management with Direct I/O, i.e., the anti-mmap design point)
core_idea: F2 evolves FASTER's single HybridLog into a two-tier design: a hot log (in-memory mutable region for write-hot records, FASTER-style hash index) and a cold log (almost fully disk-resident) with a memory-frugal two-level cold index (in-memory chunk index + on-disk 256B hash chunks, <1 byte of RAM per cold key), plus an in-memory read-cache for disk-resident read-hot records (Sec 4, 6, 7). A new latch-free Conditional-Insert primitive enables multi-threaded lookup-based log compaction that avoids FASTER's scan-based compaction's memory spikes and "death spiral" (Sec 3.2, 5).
relation_to_vmemkv: Direct competitor in VMemKV's exact target regime (point-op KV, dataset 10-40x larger than memory, skewed access, constrained memory), published PVLDB 2025 and open-source. It is the strongest recent representative of the opposite design philosophy: explicit user-space memory management + Direct I/O + latch-free concurrency vs. VMemKV's OS-delegated mmap residency.
same_as_vmemkv: (1) Two-tier separation with a RAM-resident index/control structure over disk-resident data (F2 hot-log index + cold-log two-level index vs VMemKV T1). (2) Garbage collection by copying live records to a new location and truncating, instead of LSM leveled compaction (F2 lookup-based compaction, Sec 5.2 vs VMemKV T2 reorganization). (3) Target workload: point Get/Insert/Update/Delete on larger-than-memory skewed data with limited RAM (Sec 1, 2).
different_from_vmemkv: (1) Residency control: F2 explicitly manages memory (HybridLog regions, read-cache, 32MiB circular compaction buffers) and uses Direct I/O; VMemKV delegates T2 residency to OS paging via mmap. (2) Index: F2 is hash-only, unordered, no scans; VMemKV T1 has a sorted region enabling ordered Scan. (3) Tiering axis: F2 tiers by record hotness (hot/cold records); VMemKV tiers by role (metadata vs values). (4) F2 keeps cold-record index mostly on disk (<1B RAM/key, Sec 6); VMemKV keeps ALL per-key metadata in RAM (~32B/entry T1).
evaluated_workloads: All in Sec 8: (a) Motivation case study: uniform random read-only, 30GiB DB / 1GiB buffer, 4KiB random reads, thread sweep and RAID-0 disk-count sweep (Sec 2.1, Fig 1). (b) FASTER death-spiral demo: larger-than-memory YCSB-F RMW over time (Sec 3.2, Fig 3). (c) Compaction microbenchmark: compact 2GiB of a 30GiB log, scan- vs lookup-based, 1-8 threads (Sec 8.2, Fig 9). (d) Read-cache sizing sweep on YCSB-B/C (Sec 8.2, text only).
baselines: FASTER (original, but with F2's lookup-based compaction substituted to stay within memory budget), RocksDB v8.11.4 (Bloom filters 10 bits, data-block hash index, OptimizeForPointLookup), SplinterDB commit 1939a12 (quotient filters on), KVell commit af10b7a, LeanStore commit 26d4a46 io branch.
metrics: Average throughput Kreqs/s (Sec 8.1, Figs 10-13); block-read KIOPS vs theoretical max 580 KIOPS/disk (Fig 1); throughput over time during compaction (Fig 3); compaction disk-read MiB/s and completion time (Fig 9); peak memory during compaction (Sec 8.2: 120MiB vs 3GiB); single-thread average read/write latency in microseconds (Table 1);
value_sizes: YCSB: 8B keys, 100B values (Sec 8.1). MixGraph: 48B keys, variable-sized values per Meta's models (Sec 8.1); exact value distribution not specified. No large-value (KiB-scale) experiments.
dataset_size_or_memory_ratio: 250M keys => ~30GiB YCSB dataset, ~40GiB MixGraph (implied by 4GiB=10%). Default memory budget = 10% of dataset (3GiB YCSB, 4GiB MixGraph), i.e. 10x larger-than-memory (Sec 8.1). Memory sweep: 750MiB-7.5GiB = 2.5-25% of DB, i.e. 4x-40x larger-than-memory (Sec 8.5, Fig 13). Motivation study: 30GiB DB / 1GiB buffer = 30x (Sec 2.1, Fig 1).
access_distribution: Zipfian with YCSB default theta=0.99 (equivalently alpha=1/(1-theta)=100; 90% of accesses hit 18% of records) (Sec 8.1); skew sweep alpha in [3,1000], where alpha=10 means 90% of accesses hit 33% of keys (Sec 8.1, 8.4, Fig 12); YCSB-D read-latest distribution (Sec 8.1);
scan_or_range_support: Not supported and not evaluated. F2 supports only point Reads, Upserts, Deletes, RMWs (Sec 4); it is hash-indexed with no ordered structure. The 3% seek ops in MixGraph were explicitly skipped (Sec 8.1). This is a stated scope limitation, not measured.
update_workload: Yes, central: YCSB-A 50% updates, custom YCSB-W 95% updates (blind upserts), YCSB-F 50% RMWs, YCSB-D 5% inserts (Sec 8.1, Fig 10); RMW algorithm with Conditional-Insert detailed in Sec 5.3/Algorithm 1; Fig 3 shows FASTER's RMW death-spiral. Updates to in-memory mutable-region records are in-place;
larger_than_memory_setting: The entire paper is a larger-than-memory study: default 10x (memory = 10% of dataset, cgroup-enforced, Sec 8.1); explicit sweep from 4x to 40x larger-than-memory (2.5-25% budgets, Sec 8.5, Fig 13); 30x in the Fig 1 motivation. Memory limits enforced both via each system's config knobs and Linux cgroups (Sec 8.1).
reason: The strongest measured occupant of VMemKV target regime (point ops, Zipf, 10-40x LTM). Cite its numbers honestly; adopt memory-%-sweep, skew sweep, RA/WA-per-experiment (/proc/pid/io), %-of-device-IOPS reporting. Direct comparison optional (appendix) because F2 has no scans; scope statement must be explicit.
thesis_strengthening_points: (1) Complexity cost of the explicit-management alternative: F2 needs ~11k SLOC (Sec 4.3), a new latch-free Conditional-Insert primitive (Sec 5.1), a false-absence anomaly fix (Sec 5.4), a hand-built read-cache with second-chance eviction (Sec 7), and per-workload sizing guidelines (Sec 4.3) - exactly the machinery VMemKV claims to delegate to the OS. This directly feeds VMemKV's implementation-responsibility table. (2) F2 never evaluates values larger than ~100B (Sec 8.1);
thesis_weakening_points: Be blunt: F2 is the single most dangerous related work for VMemKV. (1) Empirical bar: in VMemKV's exact target regime (point ops, Zipfian, 10x larger-than-memory), F2 hits 2400-3500 Kreqs/s at 16 threads and saturates 85-90% of a 4-disk NVMe RAID (Sec 8.3, Figs 10-11). mmap fault-driven reads are known (Crotty et al., and implied by F2's Direct I/O choice) to cap far below device IOPS due to 4KiB-granularity faults, page-table/TLB overheads, and single-threaded kernel reclaim; if VMemKV's numbers are an order of magnitude below F2's on comparable hardware, 'practical performance' collapses to 'practical only where nobody measured F2', and a reviewer WILL know F2's numbers.
reviewer_risk_if_omitted: Severe. paper: Bitcask: A Log-Structured Hash Table for Fast Key/Value Data
system_or_method: Bitcask: the local storage engine developed for the Riak distributed database. An in-memory hash table ("keydir") maps every key to a fixed-size record (file id, offset, size) of the latest entry; values live in append-only immutable data files on disk; deletes are tombstone appends;
category: Hybrid-log KVS: in-memory hash index + append-only on-disk log ("log-structured hash table"); direct design ancestor of VMemKV and the primary anticipation/novelty threat.
core_idea: Keep a complete per-key index in RAM (keydir hash table) and store all values in append-only immutable files on disk, so every read costs at most one disk seek and writes are purely sequential appends (pages 2-3). Rely on the OS filesystem read-ahead cache for read performance instead of a user-space cache (pages 3-4). Reclaim superseded/deleted entries with an offline merge over immutable files, producing hint files that make startup keydir reconstruction fast (page 4). The data files double as the commit log, so crash recovery needs no replay (page 5).
relation_to_vmemkv: Ancestor and the single biggest anticipation threat. Bitcask (2010) already combines VMemKV's three headline ingredients: RAM-resident per-key control plane (keydir ~ T1), on-disk value log whose residency is delegated to the OS cache (data files ~ T2), and garbage-reclaiming rewrite instead of LSM compaction (merge ~ T2 reorganization). It also explicitly claims larger-than-RAM operation without degradation and simplicity as design goals (page 1).
same_as_vmemkv: (1) RAM-resident index over all keys pointing into on-disk value storage: keydir maps every key to fixed-size (file, offset, size) entries (page 3) ~ VMemKV T1 fixed-size entries with T2 offsets. (2) Explicit reliance on the OS for read caching/residency: "we rely on the operating system's filesystem cache for read performance... unclear how much [an internal read cache] will pay off" (page 4) ~ VMemKV's OS-delegated T2 page residency with no user-space buffer pool. (3) Deletes as tombstones removed at merge (page 2) ~ T1 tombstones cleared at reorganization.
different_from_vmemkv: (1) Keydir is a pure hash table: no ordering, no range scans — the API offers only get/put/delete/list_keys/fold (full iteration, page 6); VMemKV's sorted_region enables ordered Scan (YCSB-E). (2) Bitcask reads values via explicit file reads relying on OS read-ahead, not mmap (page 3); VMemKV mmaps T2, exposing it to page-fault/TLB behavior Bitcask never faces. (3) Bitcask never updates in place — every put is an append to the active file (page 2); VMemKV updates in place when new_value_len <= alloc_len. (4) Bitcask keeps the full key both in data-file entries and keydir;
evaluated_workloads: Essentially none in any rigorous sense. The paper contains NO figures, tables, or numbered experiments. It reports only "early tests"/"initial simple benchmarking" (pages 4-5): (a) an unspecified write stream test "on a laptop with slow disks" yielding 5000-6000 writes/sec (page 5); (b) the same tests used "a dataset of more than 10x RAM" (page 5); (c) unspecified latency tests showing "sub-millisecond typical median latency" (page 5). Workload composition, key/value sizes, read/write mix, and distributions are all unspecified. Benchmarks "against various API-similar local storage systems" are promised "very soon" but not included (page 4).
baselines: No quantitative baselines. Berkeley DB, Tokyo Cabinet, and Innostore are named only as qualitatively-evaluated alternatives against the goal list (page 1); the claim "Bitcask handily outperform[s] other fast storage systems for many scenarios" carries no data (page 4).
metrics: All anecdotal, no figures/tables: median write/read latency ("sub-millisecond typical median latency (and quite adequate higher percentiles)", page 5); write throughput (5000-6000 writes/sec, page 5); keydir memory footprint ("well under a GB of memory" for "many millions of keys", page 5); qualitative claims of single-disk-seek reads (page 3) and fast startup via hint files (pages 4-5).
dataset_size_or_memory_ratio: "more than 10x RAM" for the early tests (page 5); total volumes tested "so far it has only seen double-digit gigabyte volumes" (page 5). Absolute RAM size and exact dataset size not specified.
access_distribution: Not formally specified. The design goal mentions "writing an incoming stream of random items" (page 1); no Zipf/uniform/hotset characterization anywhere.
scan_or_range_support: No range queries: the keydir is an unordered hash table. Only list_keys (all keys) and fold (over all K/V pairs) are provided (API table, page 6). Not evaluated at all.
update_workload: Not evaluated as a distinct workload. By design every put (update or insert) is a blind append to the active file with a keydir pointer swap (pages 2-3); there is no in-place update path and no read-modify-write discussion.
larger_than_memory_setting: Claimed but not demonstrated with data: "The tests mentioned above used a dataset of more than 10x RAM... and showed no sign of changed behavior at that point. This is consistent with our expectations given the design" (page 5). No curves, no fault/IO measurements, no working-set variation — a one-sentence anecdote.
reason: Anticipation threat, not a runnable modern baseline (whitepaper system; Erlang/Riak ecosystem). The pread twin is the runnable proxy answering "why mmap instead of Bitcask-style pread". Adopt: >=10x ratio point, sustained ingest, startup time, T1 bytes/key vs keydir full-key footprint.
thesis_strengthening_points: (1) Bitcask validates the general design point: OS-delegated value residency plus a RAM index shipped in production Riak and met its goals (pages 1, 5), so VMemKV's hypothesis is not eccentric. (2) Bitcask's evaluation vacuum is VMemKV's opportunity: the whitepaper has zero figures/tables, "early tests on a laptop with slow disks", and benchmarks that were only "promised soon" (pages 4-5).
thesis_weakening_points: (1) Novelty collapse risk: strip the sorted region and mmap, and VMemKV IS Bitcask — RAM index with fixed-size entries pointing at an on-disk value log, OS-managed read residency, tombstones, copying merge reclaiming garbage, "simple implementation" as an explicit goal (pages 1-4). The remaining delta (sorted T1 region for scans, mmap instead of read(), in-place update within alloc_len, Inline64) must carry the entire novelty argument. (2) The headline claim "OS-delegated larger-than-memory value residency works" was already asserted by Bitcask at >10x RAM in 2010 (page 5); VMemKV planning only 4x/8x could look weaker than a 15-year-old anecdote unless it exceeds or explains the ratio.
reviewer_risk_if_omitted: Severe. Any storage reviewer knows Bitcask; if VMemKV does not cite and differentiate it, the near-certain first review comment is "this is Bitcask with a sorted index and mmap — the design is not new" and the paper gets rejected on novelty regardless of evaluation quality. Specific objections a reviewer will raise: (a) OS-delegated residency for larger-than-RAM values is Bitcask's page-4 design decision verbatim; (b) tombstone + copying merge is Bitcask's merge, so 'reorganization instead of LSM compaction' cannot be presented as a new alternative to compaction;
implementation_feasibility: Custom Bitcask-like baseline: medium but fairness-explanation cost high; pread twin preferred.
needs_verification: whitepaper has no venue; cite as Basho Technologies technical whitepaper, 2010
notes: This is a 6-page company whitepaper, not a peer-reviewed paper: no numbered sections, no figures or tables in the text layer (diagrams exist as images between paragraphs), no references section, no methodology. All performance claims are self-described as "early"/"initial simple benchmarking" with benchmarks "against various API-similar local storage systems" promised but never included (page 4).

paper: Bigtable: A Distributed Storage System for Structured Data
system_or_method: Bigtable: a distributed, sparse, multi-dimensional sorted map over row/column/timestamp, built on GFS + Chubby, served by tablet servers using a memtable + immutable SSTables + commit log architecture with minor/merging/major compactions.
category: Distributed storage / LSM lineage origin (memtable+SSTable+compaction design that LevelDB and RocksDB descend from)
core_idea: Bigtable provides a simple sorted-map data model (row key, column key, timestamp -> uninterpreted bytes) that scales to petabytes across thousands of commodity servers (Abstract, Sec 2). Each tablet is served from a persistent redo commit log plus an in-memory sorted memtable and a sequence of immutable on-disk SSTables; reads merge memtable and SSTables, and minor/merging/major compactions bound the number of SSTables and reclaim deleted data (Sec 5.3-5.4). Clients control locality and memory residency explicitly via schemas, locality groups, and in-memory locality groups (Sec 2, Sec 6).
relation_to_vmemkv: Ancestor / Related Work anchor. It is the origin of the memtable+SSTable+compaction lineage that VMemKV's baseline (RocksDB) descends from, and the reference point for VMemKV's "reorganization instead of LSM compaction" framing. It also contains two design precedents directly relevant to VMemKV: (1) SSTables can be "completely mapped into memory" via mmap to serve lookups/scans without touching disk (Sec 4);
same_as_vmemkv: (a) VMemKV's T1 append_region (recent inserts) + sorted_region (binary search) mirrors Bigtable's memtable (recent writes) + sorted SSTables, and T1 reorganization mirrors merging compaction; T2 reorganization that copies live records into a new file and drops garbage is functionally Bigtable's major compaction, which "produces an SSTable that contains no deletion information or deleted data" (Sec 5.4).
different_from_vmemkv: Bigtable is a distributed multi-node system on GFS/Chubby with tablets, a master, and load balancing (Sec 4-5); VMemKV is single-node. Bigtable's SSTables are immutable and multi-versioned by timestamp; VMemKV's T2 does in-place updates when alloc_len permits. Bigtable is durable by design: every mutation goes to a redo commit log with group commit before entering the memtable (Sec 5.3), and recovery replays from redo points; VMemKV's current implementation has no WAL/msync and is explicitly non-durable.
evaluated_workloads: All in Section 7 (Performance Evaluation), results in Figure 6 (p.9): (1) sequential writes (row keys 0..R-1 partitioned into 10N ranges, one random uncompressible string per key); (2) random writes (same but row key hashed modulo R, uniform spread); (3) sequential reads (reads back keys written by sequential write); (4) random reads (shadows random write pattern; each read fetches a 64 KB SSTable block from GFS for one 1000-byte value); (5) random reads (mem) (same but locality group marked in-memory, data reduced from 1 GB to 100 MB per server); (6) scans (all values in a row range via Scanner API, single RPC fetches large value sequences). Each run at N = 1, 50, 250, 500 tablet servers.
baselines: None. No comparison against any other system; the evaluation is Bigtable-only scaling from 1 to 500 tablet servers (Sec 7, Fig 6). Related work (Sec 10) compares qualitatively to Boxwood, DHTs, parallel DBs, C-Store, LSM-tree.
metrics: Number of 1000-byte values read/written per second, reported both per tablet server (Fig 6 table) and aggregate across the cluster (Fig 6 graph) (Sec 7). Derived GFS bandwidth (~75 MB/s for random reads at 1200 ops/s, Sec 7 "Single tablet-server performance"). No latency measurements, no percentiles/tail latency in the benchmark section.
value_sizes: 1000-byte values for all six benchmarks (Sec 7, Fig 6 caption: "Number of 1000-byte values read/written per second"). Production tables have varied average cell sizes (Table 2 gives table sizes and cell counts, not explicit value sizes).
dataset_size_or_memory_ratio: R chosen so each benchmark reads/writes ~1 GB of data per tablet server; tablet servers configured with 1 GB of memory (Sec 7), i.e., dataset roughly ~1x server memory but stored remotely in GFS (1786 machines, two 400 GB IDE drives each), not demand-paged locally.
access_distribution: Uniform: random write hashes the row key modulo R "so that the write load was spread roughly uniformly across the entire row space" (Sec 7); random read shadows the random write pattern. Sequential benchmarks use keys 0..R-1 in order. No Zipf/skewed distribution anywhere in the evaluation.
scan_or_range_support: Yes. Scanner API iterates over row ranges with column/timestamp filtering (Sec 3, Fig 3). Scan benchmark evaluated: fastest operation at 15,385 values/s per server (single server), 7,843 values/s per server at 500 servers (Fig 6), because one RPC returns many values, amortizing RPC overhead (Sec 7). [...]
update_workload: Writes in the benchmarks are blind writes of a single string per row key (sequential and random writes, Sec 7); the read benchmarks re-read previously written data, so writes act as overwrites on repeat runs but no explicit update/RMW benchmark exists.
larger_than_memory_setting: Indirectly. The main benchmarks use ~1 GB data per tablet server against 1 GB configured server memory, with data stored on GFS and fetched as 64 KB blocks per read, so random reads are disk/network-bound rather than page-fault-bound (Sec 7).
reason: Distributed system, out of scope as baseline. Cite as LSM lineage origin; acknowledge mmap-mapped SSTables (Sec 4) and its explicit choice of user-directed (not dynamic/OS) memory residency (Sec 10) when framing novelty.
thesis_strengthening_points: (1) Sec 9's most important lesson is "the value of simple designs" for maintainability and debugging — direct rhetorical support for VMemKV's simplicity claim. (2) Sec 10 concedes the key-value model "lends itself to a very efficient flat-file representation," consistent with VMemKV's flat T2 file. (3) The 64 KB-block-per-1000-byte-read amplification story (Sec 7) motivates VMemKV's finer-grained access: OS 4 KiB page granularity is 16x finer than Bigtable's default block, so VMemKV can argue page-granular residency reduces read amplification for point lookups relative to block/SSTable-granula [...]
thesis_weakening_points: (1) Strongest: Bigtable explicitly rejected automatic memory-residency decisions — "we let the user tell us what data belongs in memory and what data should stay on disk, rather than trying to determine this dynamically" (Sec 10) — and built explicit in-memory locality groups plus its own user-space Scan/Block caches (Sec 6) instead of relying on any generic caching layer. A reviewer can cite the LSM lineage's founding paper as evidence that experienced builders considered and declined exactly the delegation VMemKV proposes; VMemKV must show OS delegation wins, not merely simplifies. (2) Novelty risk on mmap: Sec 4 already offered fully memory-mapped SSTables in 2006;
reviewer_risk_if_omitted: High for Related Work, low as an empirical baseline. Any OSDI/SOSP-track reviewer will expect Bigtable [Chang et al., OSDI 2006] cited as the origin of the memtable/SSTable/compaction lineage the moment VMemKV says "instead of LSM compaction"; omitting it (citing only O'Neil's LSM-tree or RocksDB) looks careless. paper: Predictive Translation: High-Performance Buffer Management Without the Trade-Offs
system_or_method: PrediCache — a from-scratch C++ buffer pool prototype implementing "predictive translation": a chaining hash table (inlined first slot, inlined frame headers, optimistic latches) that maps PIDs to buffer frames, plus deterministic "preferred position" placement of hot pages so the CPU's superscalar/ [...]
category: Buffer manager (user-space, hash-table-based) for larger-than-memory storage engines; direct competitor/critic of OS-assisted caching (vmcache) and mmap-based designs (LMDB)
core_idea: The paper challenges the belief that hash-table-based buffer pools are inherently slow. It assigns each PID a deterministic "preferred" buffer frame (hash of PID mod pool size) and probabilistically promotes hot pages into it (probability 1/32, or 1/512 if a demotion is needed; Sec 5.1), so the CPU can speculatively read the predicted frame while the lock-free hash-table translation is still in flight, hiding translation latency via superscalar execution (Sec 3, Listings 1-3).
relation_to_vmemkv: Adversarial competitor philosophy + methodology source. It comes from the same TUM group as vmcache, LeanStore, and the "Are You Sure You Want to Use MMAP?" criticism [27], and it argues the current best answer to larger-than-memory residency is a well-engineered USER-SPACE buffer pool — the opposite of VMemKV's OS-delegated T2 residency. Its LMDB out-of-memory result (Sec 6.2) is a direct empirical attack on VMemKV's architecture class.
same_as_vmemkv: (1) Both claim "simple implementation + high performance" as the core contribution and both frame practicality/portability (no kernel modules, no invasive index changes) as first-class design goals (Sec 2.2, Table 1) — the same rhetorical position VMemKV takes. (2) Both keep a RAM-resident control/translation structure whose metadata scales with what is cached/keyed rather than with total storage (PrediCache: frame headers inlined in hash table, Sec 4.1, Fig 12; VMemKV: T1 entries).
different_from_vmemkv: (1) PrediCache is a page-granularity user-space buffer pool with explicit eviction and direct I/O under a B-tree DBMS; VMemKV has NO buffer pool and delegates T2 value-page residency entirely to the OS page cache via mmap. (2) PrediCache caches fixed 4KB pages of a B-tree; VMemKV stores variable-size value records in a log-like T2 file plus a separate fixed-entry T1 index. category: Buffer manager (production-grade, many-core scalable, disk-based DBMS; explicit user-space page cache — the design-space opposite of OS-delegated residency)
core_idea: Traditional DBMS buffer managers bottleneck on centralized per-buffer reference counting, shared page latches, and lock-protected chained hash tables for page-to-buffer translation; Figure 1 shows these consume >60% of index query latency on a 128-core server. Radical alternatives (pointer swizzling, vmcache's virtual-memory-assisted buffer pool, optimistic latching with retries) are argued to be unusable in production due to incompatibility, page-table memory consumption, and retry hazards (out-of-bounds reads, signal handling).

(c) Durability: GaussDB has full WAL/recovery in production; VMemKV's current implementation is checkpoint-free with MAP_PRIVATE.

paper: LLFree: Scalable and Optionally-Persistent Page-Frame Allocation
system_or_method: LLFree: a lock- and log-free physical page-frame allocator (replacement for the Linux buddy allocator), implemented in ~2199 lines of safe Rust, integrated into Linux 6.0, with optional crash consistency on NVRAM (eADR).
category: OS page allocator (kernel physical-memory management), with optional persistent-memory crash consistency
core_idea: The Linux buddy allocator scales poorly (global zone lock, scattered struct-page-based free lists, expensive 4KiB-to-2MiB merges), fragments huge frames, and cannot be made persistent without heavy logging. LLFree replaces it with a two-level cache-line-centric design: a lower level of per-huge-frame 16-bit counters plus 512-bit bit fields in flat arrays (every de/allocation commits atomically in a single cache line, giving log-free crash consistency on eADR NVRAM), and a volatile upper level of 64 MiB "trees" with per-CPU tree reservation and a reserve-on-free heuristic to avoid sharing and t [...]
relation_to_vmemkv: Peripheral, but not irrelevant: LLFree sits inside the exact kernel page-fault/allocation path that VMemKV delegates T2 residency to. It is (a) a source of evidence about what the OS-side page-fault path actually costs and where its bottlenecks are (Fig 13 flame graph: page allocator only 5.3% of a page-fault-heavy write workload; mmap rw-lock 17.3%;
same_as_vmemkv: Shared philosophy points only: (1) "simplicity" argued partly via lines of code (2199 lines of Rust + 1318 test lines vs 6060+ lines in Linux page_alloc.c, Sec 4.1) — same rhetorical move as VMemKV's implementation-responsibility table. (2) Avoiding logging by making each state transition a single atomic cache-line commit and reconstructing derived state on recovery (Sec 3.2.3) — conceptually similar to VMemKV's "checkpoint-free" stance of rebuilding/relying on authoritative structures rather than write-ahead logs.
different_from_vmemkv: Different layer entirely: LLFree manages physical page frames inside the kernel; VMemKV is a userspace KV store that consumes the paging subsystem via mmap. LLFree has no notion of keys, values, Get/Scan, persistence of user data (its persistence is for allocator metadata on NVRAM with eADR, not for file-backed data via msync/WAL). Its evaluation is allocator micro/synthetic benchmarks plus memtier/memcached and a page-fault write benchmark — no YCSB, no larger-than-memory paging to SSD, no value sizes, no skewed distributions.
evaluated_workloads: (1) Three synthetic allocator benchmarks — bulk (all cores allocate half of memory then free), random (allocate all, free in random order, only frees measured), repeat (each core alloc+free single frame, best case for Linux per-CPU caches) (Sec 5.1). (2) Per-order allocation sizes 4 KiB–4 MiB, 8 cores, 128 GiB DRAM and DAX-mapped Optane, userspace standalone (Fig 5) and in-kernel (Fig 6) (Sec 5.2). (3) Multicore scalability 1–26 cores, orders 0 and 9, 128 GiB, userspace DRAM/NVRAM (Fig 7) and in-kernel (Fig 8) (Sec 5.3). (4) List-based allocator comparison ListLocked/ListCAS/ListLocal, order 0, 128 GiB (Fig 9, Sec 5.4). (5) State-dispersion accounting (Tab 1, Sec 5.5).
baselines: Linux 6.0 buddy allocator (in-situ replacement, Sec 4.2, Secs 5.2–5.8); three prototypical list-based allocators: ListLocked (Windows/Darwin-style locked free list), ListCAS (Treiber lock-free LIFO list), ListLocal (idealized per-core-lists-only allocator) (Sec 5.4, Fig 9).

value_sizes: Not applicable / not specified — no KV value sizes; allocation sizes are page-frame orders 0–10 (4 KiB–4 MiB) (Sec 5.2, Fig 5/6). memtier request sizes are not specified in the paper.
dataset_size_or_memory_ratio: Allocator benchmarks operate on 128 GiB of a 256 GiB DRAM machine or DAX-mapped Optane (Secs 5.2–5.4, 5.7, 5.8); fragmentation benchmark uses a 125 GiB region at 90% allocation (Sec 5.6). No dataset/memory ratio in the KVS sense; nothing exceeds physical memory.

scan_or_range_support: Not applicable — no scans/range queries; the closest analogue is full-state enumeration for the state-dispersion metric (Sec 5.5, Tab 1) and recovery iteration over bit fields (Sec 5.7).

system_or_method: Value-separated variant of RocksDB: values above min_blob_size stored in blob files outside the LSM, with blob garbage collection during compaction.
core_idea: Productionized WiscKey-style key-value separation inside RocksDB; keys and blob references stay in the LSM, large values live in blob files, GC rewrites blob files based on garbage ratio.
relation_to_vmemkv: The runnable, production value-separated LSM that makes 16 KiB comparisons fair; the practical stand-in for WiscKey.
same_as_vmemkv: Value separation; index holds references to out-of-LSM value storage; garbage collection of dead values.
different_from_vmemkv: Explicit I/O + block cache (no mmap residency delegation); durable (WAL); GC integrated with compaction rather than whole-generation reorganization.
evaluated_workloads: n/a (no standalone paper; documented in RocksDB wiki/blog)
scan_or_range_support: yes (LSM iterators; scans dereference blob files)
reason: Without a value-separated RocksDB configuration at 16 KiB, beating vanilla RocksDB re-proves WiscKey 2016 rather than testing VMemKV. Config: enable_blob_files, min_blob_size, blob GC settings must be reported.
thesis_strengthening_points: If VMemKV is competitive with BlobDB at matched memory while carrying fewer engine responsibilities, the design-point claim gains real support.
thesis_weakening_points: If BlobDB dominates at 16 KiB, the large-value niche is already served by a production system and the paper reduces to a characterization of mmap costs.

system_or_method: Copy-on-write B+tree stored entirely in a single mmap region; readers lock-free via MVCC snapshots; single writer.
core_idea: Map the whole database file and let the OS page cache manage residency; shadow-paging gives crash consistency without a WAL; famous for read performance and simplicity.
relation_to_vmemkv: The mmap incumbent. VMemKV differs by mmapping only the value plane (T1 stays a RAM structure) and by write path (LMDB is CoW append; VMemKV in-place + append).
same_as_vmemkv: OS-managed residency via mmap; simplicity as an explicit selling point.
different_from_vmemkv: Whole-tree mmap vs value-only mmap; single-writer; durable by design (MDB_NOSYNC optional); ordered B+tree native scans.
evaluated_workloads: Evaluated as baseline in vmcache (Sec 5.1-5.3) and Predictive Translation (Sec 6.1-6.3): random lookups, TPC-C, in/out-of-memory; PrediCache Fig 6 shows its out-of-memory collapse.
dataset_size_or_memory_ratio: ~1 TB vs 128 GB pool in vmcache/PrediCache setups
larger_than_memory_setting: yes (loses badly per vmcache Fig 6-7, PrediCache Fig 6)
reason: mmap incumbent; cheap to integrate (mature C library); promotes from appendix to at least one main-text figure (Get/Scan/LTM). Not a primary rival (B+tree, single-writer) but the natural diagnostic for "is VMemKV just mmap?".
thesis_strengthening_points: If VMemKV beats LMDB out-of-memory thanks to RAM-resident T1 (no faults on index pages), the T1/T2 split earns direct evidence.
thesis_weakening_points: If VMemKV reproduces the LMDB cliff, the delegation thesis narrows further.
reviewer_risk_if_omitted: Medium-high: a paper positioning itself among mmap KVSs that never measures the canonical one.
implementation_feasibility: High (liblmdb packaged everywhere; small C API).
needs_verification: Canonical citation (Chu, LADIS/MDB report vs software reference) - Needs verification.
notes: Not in must_read_papers (appears as baseline inside vmcache.pdf / predictive-translation.pdf).

core_idea: Defines update-heavy (A), read-heavy (B), read-only (C), read-latest (D), short-scan (E), RMW (F) mixes with Zipfian/latest/uniform request distributions.

reason: Necessary common vocabulary but insufficient alone: says nothing about eviction onset, WA, page faults, reorganization, recovery.
thesis_weakening_points: Relying on YCSB alone would hide every mmap-specific failure mode.
